answer.rationale:
The binding constraint is not cost alone but cost subject to zero added delivery risk: the line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days. Any action that introduces migration, qualification, or first-article risk in that window is asymmetric — a small supply miss costs more than the 18% it might save. That rules switch_primary_vendor out as a primary move this cycle and rules defer_decision out as well, since deferral here is not a benign month-to-month drift (memory_c5 concerned a non-critical service) but a lapse of the primary supply agreement. add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right structural move but is a next-cycle action; qualifying a second source takes longer than 14 days and does not deliver this year's savings.

That leaves negotiate_terms as the one action that attacks TCO without touching the physical supply chain: memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and memory_c6 says a multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope. Combining the two — benchmark-anchored renegotiation with a term extension traded for volume pricing — is the plausible path to a material fraction of the 18%, with memory_c1's integration stability as the fallback if talks stall.

Verification is aimed at the two memories that most move the decision. memory_c2 is the strongest apparent argument for switching, and it is exactly the kind of record I distrust: it reports unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy but is silent on on-time delivery, defect rates, and whether the switch happened while there was slack in the line. I need the original record to know whether that win is transferable to a no-buffer, 14-day situation or whether it was won under conditions we do not have. memory_c4 sets my expected negotiation yield; if the recovered margin was a few points rather than double digits, negotiation alone will not clear the 18% mandate and I must go in planning a term-for-price trade (c6) plus a scoped volume rebalance, and flag the shortfall to finance rather than pretend the target is met.

Risk to note explicitly: this inherited memory set is six consolidated success stories with no recorded failures, and each one endorses a different action. That is a survivorship pattern, not a body of evidence — the sessions that switched vendors and got burned, or negotiated and got nothing, are not represented. I am treating these as hypotheses about what has worked, not as settled facts, and I am deliberately choosing the reversible action: a negotiation that fails leaves us where we are, whereas a switch that fails stops the line. I hold the 18% target as genuinely uncertain of achievement this cycle and will not overstate confidence to finance to make the number look met.
